analysis.one_liner: Caps prison and jail phone rates at a few cents per minute and bans the commissions prisons take from phone companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce subcommittee from April 2021 until the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The Martha Wright Prison Phone Justice Act — named for a grandmother who had to choose between her medication and calls to her incarcerated grandson — would have required the Federal Communications Commission to set maximum rates for phone calls from jails and prisons, capped rates at 4–5 cents per minute in the meantime, and ended the practice of prison phone companies paying "site commissions" to the facilities that pick them. It died without even a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The families of the roughly two million people in U.S. jails and prisons, who pay for the calls. Prison phone calls have long cost far more than ordinary calls — often over a dollar a minute — and the people paying are overwhelmingly low-income families, disproportionately women and people of color. The bill's findings note that high call costs strain family bonds and are associated with higher recidivism, so cheaper calls also benefit the communities people return to [S3]. It also would have helped the incarcerated people themselves stay in touch with lawyers, family, and support systems [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families paying for calls from jail

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FCC to set maximum rates and fees for confinement facility communications services based on the average industry cost of providing them, with a review every two years [S2, S3].
Sets interim caps until FCC rules take effect: 4 cents per minute for debit or prepaid calling and 5 cents per minute for collect calls [S3].
Requires per-minute billing for the actual duration of the call and bans per-call or per-connection fees, which had inflated the effective cost of short calls [S2, S3].
Caps ancillary charges — things like automated payment fees, live-agent fees, and paper-bill fees — and requires third-party fees to be passed through with no markup [S3].

Bans 'site commissions' — payments, gifts, or in-kind benefits from phone providers to the facilities that choose them. The bill's findings state these commissions are the main criterion many facilities use to pick a provider, and that they drive rates far above actual cost [S3].
Applies to existing contracts, which could not be extended, and bars states from allowing rates higher than the federal caps [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Prison phone companies, which have operated local monopolies at jails and prisons and charged families some of the highest call rates in the country, would lose the bulk of that margin, plus the site-commission payments they use to win contracts. State and local corrections agencies and jails would lose the commission revenue they currently collect from those contracts [S2, S3]. Taxpayers would not pay anything; the cost falls on the industry.
analysis.who_pays_short: Prison phone companies and jail budgets

drawbacks.text: The interim caps of 4–5 cents per minute could fall below the actual cost of providing monitored, secure calls at some facilities before the FCC sets cost-based rates, which the bill's own findings acknowledge are higher in confinement settings due to security needs [S3].

Phone providers might respond by cutting service quality, staffing, or technology investments, and jails that currently use commission revenue for programs or operations would have to replace it from other budgets [S2, S3].
The bill preempts state and local rules that allow higher charges, which removes a tool some jurisdictions had used to regulate the industry on their own terms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go directly to low-income families paying for calls, and the costs fall on a small, highly profitable industry and on agencies collecting commissions — not on taxpayers. The strongest honest objection is transition risk: cost-based FCC rates may be higher than the interim 4–5 cent caps, and facilities relying on commission money would feel the loss. But the bill was written so the FCC would eventually set rates on actual industry costs, which addresses the main fairness concern. On the whole, the costs are modest and concentrated; the benefit to families of incarcerated people is large and immediate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications subcommittee, and no committee ever voted on it; it sat there until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on April 13, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1, S5].
The next day it was referred to the subcommittee on Communications and Technology — the last action the bill ever received [S5].
The bill attracted 48 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats; no Republican signed on [S4].
The committee leadership never scheduled a markup or vote, and the bill never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prison phone companies kept their exclusive contracts, their high per-minute rates, and their per-call fees, and the jails and state agencies that collect site commissions kept that revenue. Families paying for calls from confinement facilities remained no better off through federal legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Prison phone companies and jail agencies

for.name: Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Martha Wright Prison Phone Justice Act on April 13, 2021.

for.name: 48 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee vote on the bill; it sat at the Communications subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Prison phone industry (providers such as Securus Technologies and Global Tel Link)
against.role: Providers of confinement facility communications services
against.what_they_did: The industry's business model — exclusive jail contracts, per-minute rates of a dollar or more, per-call fees, and site-commission payments to facilities — would have been dismantled by the bill; the industry has a long record of lobbying against rate regulation at the FCC and in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 48 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill then stalled in a committee controlled by the same party.

industries.industry: Prison phone and communications providers (Securus, Global Tel Link, and similar firms)
industries.note: These companies hold exclusive contracts with jails and prisons and charge families among the highest phone rates in the country, inflated by per-call fees and the site commissions they pay facilities to win contracts. The bill would have capped rates at 4–5 cents per minute, banned per-call fees and ancillary charges, and outlawed site commissions entirely [S2, S3].

industries.industry: State and local corrections agencies, jails, and private prison operators
industries.note: Facilities that choose the phone provider collect site commissions from it — money that comes out of what families pay for calls. The bill's findings state these commissions drive rates far above actual cost and would be banned outright, forcing agencies to replace that revenue [S2, S3].
